names.primary: The Book of Beliefs and Opinions
names.original: كتاب الأمانات والاعتقادات (Judeo-Arabic); הָאֱמוּנוֹת וְהַדֵּעוֹת / אמונות ודעות (Hebrew)

aliases: The Book of Doctrines and Beliefs

date.note: Composed in Judeo-Arabic, conventionally dated to 933 CE (a first recension is dated by Saadia himself; the work was revised). Translated into Hebrew by Judah ibn Tibbon in 1186 under the title Emunot ve-Deot, the form by which it is known in the Hebrew tradition. Written by Saadia Gaon (882-942) during his years associated with the academy of Sura in Babylonia.

summary: The Book of Beliefs and Opinions (Kitab al-Amanat wa-l-I'tiqadat, in Judah ibn Tibbon's Hebrew Emunot ve-Deot), composed in Judeo-Arabic in 933, is the treatise of Saadia Gaon generally described as the first systematic work of medieval Jewish philosophical theology. Drawing on the method and vocabulary of the Kalam, and in particular the rational theology of the Muslim Mutazila, it argues that rational inquiry rightly conducted confirms rather than contradicts revelation, and treats in turn the creation of the world, the unity of God, command and prohibition, free will, the soul, and reward and redemption.
description:
The Book of Beliefs and Opinions, in Judeo-Arabic Kitab al-Amanat wa-l-I'tiqadat and in the Hebrew translation of Judah ibn Tibbon (1186) Sefer ha-Emunot ve-ha-Deot ('the Book of Beliefs and Opinions' or 'of Doctrines and Beliefs'), is the major theological treatise of Saadia ben Joseph al-Fayyumi, known as Saadia Gaon (882-942), composed in 933. It is generally described in the scholarship as the first systematic work of medieval Jewish philosophy and theology: written in the Arabic language of the Jews of the Islamic world and drawing on the methods and terminology of the Kalam, the rational theology of the Islamic milieu, and in particular of the Mutazila, it sets out to show that reason, when rightly used, arrives at and confirms the content of the received revelation rather than standing against it. The account that follows presents the work's purpose, method, and structure as attributed features of the text and of its reception in the tradition, not as claims the editor affirms.

Saadia states the purpose of the work in his introduction, read here in the open translation on Sefaria. He opens with a blessing of 'Hashem, the God of Israel who is deserving of being considered the Clear Evident Truth, Who makes the existence of the souls of speaking creatures absolutely clear to them', so that 'corruptions disappear from them and doubts leave them, so that demonstrations become clear to them and proofs lucid' (Introduction 1). He then describes his motive: he 'saw men who were drowning in the seas of doubts and overwhelmed by the waters of confusion', and, 'inasmuch as my God has taught me some things by which I can assist them', took it as his duty 'to help them and to direct them to the truth' (Introduction 2). The aim he sets is that through the study of the book 'the belief of the believer will be strengthened and doubts will be removed from the doubter and he who believes because of tradition will believe out of in-depth study and understanding' (Introduction 2). This is Saadia's program of harmonizing reason and revelation: not to replace received belief with philosophy, but to lead the believer from faith held on tradition alone to faith confirmed by rational demonstration. Sarah Stroumsa reads the work as a Jewish practice of the rational theology (Kalam) of its age, and Colette Sirat places it at the head of the history of medieval Jewish philosophy.

The treatise is organized, after the introduction, into ten treatises (maqalat). It opens with a demonstration that the world was created in time and from nothing, and hence has a Creator; it then argues the unity and incorporeality of that Creator; it treats command and prohibition, the categories of the divine law and the reasons for the commandments; the problem of obedience and disobedience, in which Saadia defends human free will and the justice of divine reward and punishment; the nature of the soul and its fate; resurrection; and, in its closing treatises, the questions of redemption, the world to come, and right conduct in this life. The characteristic move of the work, following the Kalam pattern, is to begin from arguments for the creation of the world and to build upon that foundation the proof of God and the account of God's attributes, before turning to law, the soul, and the last things. This entry describes the work's standing as the first systematic Jewish philosophy as the position it holds in the tradition and in the scholarship, and does not itself rank it against later works; the anti-Karaite and other polemical dimensions of Saadia's wider activity belong to his biography and are treated in his own entry, not here.
editorial_notes: This entry presents the Book of Beliefs and Opinions (Emunot ve-Deot) on Judaism's own terms as Saadia Gaon's systematic treatise, generally described as the first work of medieval Jewish philosophical theology (neutrality #1, #4, #6). Its purpose (leading the believer from tradition-held faith to faith confirmed by rational demonstration), its Kalam method and Mutazilite affinity, and its ten-treatise structure (creation, the unity of God, command and prohibition, free will, obedience and disobedience, the soul, resurrection, redemption, and conduct) are DESCRIBED as attributed features of the text and its reception, not adjudicated; the harmony-of-reason-and-revelation program is given as Saadia's own attributed purpose, quoted from his introduction, not endorsed. Sources triangulate three lenses per neutrality #8-9: (a) academic historians of medieval Jewish philosophy (Colette Sirat, A History of Jewish Philosophy in the Middle Ages, Cambridge 1985; Sarah Stroumsa, 'Saadya and Jewish Kalam', in The Cambridge Companion to Medieval Jewish Philosophy, 2003, carrying the same medium rating it holds in saadia-gaon.json); (b) the PRIMARY text, open and auditable on Sefaria (the Introduction to the Book of Beliefs and Opinions, in the Saadia For All / Kleiman Creative Commons translation), read line-by-line; and (c) a contemporary Jewish scholar (Stroumsa; Sirat as a historian of the tradition's own philosophy). No encyclopedias (no Encyclopaedia Judaica, no Jewish Encyclopedia, no Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy), no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. CONFIDENCE / HONESTY: the Introduction on Sefaria is rated HIGH because sections 1-2 were READ line-by-line via the open Sefaria text API and the load-bearing lines were confirmed verbatim: the opening blessing of 'the God of Israel who is deserving of being considered the Clear Evident Truth, Who makes the existence of the souls of speaking creatures absolutely clear to them', so that 'corruptions disappear from them and doubts leave them, so that demonstrations become clear to them and proofs lucid' (Introduction 1); and Saadia's statement of purpose, that he 'saw men who were drowning in the seas of doubts', took it as his 'duty to help them and to direct them to the truth', so that through the book 'the belief of the believer will be strengthened and doubts will be removed from the doubter and he who believes because of tradition will believe out of in-depth study and understanding' (Introduction 2). Only the Introduction is open and read line-by-line; the full ten-treatise structure rests on the secondary scholarship and on the standard English translation of the whole work by Samuel Rosenblatt (Yale Judaica Series 1, 1948), which is PROPRIETARY and was NOT read here, so the account of the ten treatises carries the medium confidence of that scholarship rather than the high confidence of the open Introduction. The entry is authored as a DRAFT and is best treated as REVIEWED, since only the Introduction of the primary was read line-by-line while the body of the work is known through a proprietary translation and secondary scholarship. Sirat, Stroumsa, and the Rosenblatt translation record are medium, verified to exist and be on-topic via publisher and library records, not read line-by-line. RELATION TARGETS: saadia-gaon is the author (its articulated edge points back to this work); kalam is the Islamic rational-theology method the work adopts, described as a cross-tradition related_to.

relations.note: The Book of Beliefs and Opinions (Kitab al-Amanat wa-l-I'tiqadat, Hebrew Emunot ve-Deot) was composed by Saadia Gaon (882-942), head of the academy of Sura, in 933; its introduction was read line-by-line on open Sefaria. The saadia-gaon figure entry records the reciprocal articulated edge to this work.

The work is composed in the method and vocabulary of the Kalam, the rational theology of the Islamic milieu, and in particular draws on the Muslim Mutazila, beginning (in the Kalam pattern) from arguments for the creation of the world in time and building upon it the proof of God and the account of the divine attributes. This is a cross-tradition relation: kalam is documented in the Islamic material, and the connection is stated as Saadia's adopted method, not as an equation of the two traditions. The kalam concept is documented in the Islamic tradition's material.

sources.citation: The Book of Beliefs and Opinions (HaEmunot veHaDeot), Introduction, sections 1-2; composed 933. Open Hebrew and English text on Sefaria (Saadia For All: A Creative Commons Translation of the Introduction to Emunot Vdeot by Zachary Kleiman). Cited as the openly-auditable primary text for Saadia's stated purpose and method, read line-by-line and quoted verbatim: the opening blessing of 'Hashem, the God of Israel who is deserving of being considered the Clear Evident Truth, Who makes the existence of the souls of speaking creatures absolutely clear to them', so that 'corruptions disappear from them and doubts leave them, so that demonstrations become clear to them and proofs lucid' (Introduction 1); and the statement of purpose, that Saadia 'saw men who were drowning in the seas of doubts', took it as his 'duty to help them and to direct them to the truth', so that 'the belief of the believer will be strengthened and doubts will be removed from the doubter and he who believes because of tradition will believe out of in-depth study and understanding' (Introduction 2). These lines are the load-bearing text for the work's harmony-of-reason-and-revelation program. Only the open Introduction was read line-by-line; the body of the work (the ten treatises) is not open on Sefaria.

New Haven: Yale University Press, 1948 (ISBN 9780300044904). The standard English translation of the complete work, from the introduction through the ten treatises (creation, the unity of God, command and prohibition, obedience and disobedience and free will, merits and demerits, the soul and death, resurrection, redemption, the world to come, and right conduct); cited as the reference for the full structure of the treatise beyond the open Introduction. PROPRIETARY: not open and NOT read line-by-line here, so the account of the ten treatises carries this medium rating rather than the high confidence of the open Introduction. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Yale University Press record).

Sirat, Colette. A History of Jewish Philosophy in the Middle Ages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, and Paris: Editions de la Maison des Sciences de l'Homme, 1985. The standard single-volume academic history of medieval Jewish philosophy, which opens its treatment of the philosophical tradition with Saadia Gaon and the Book of Beliefs and Opinions as the first systematic Jewish philosophy of the medieval period; cited as the academic-historian lens on the work's place and structure. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Cambridge University Press record), not read line-by-line.
